## Russia Sold Alaska for 2 Cents an Acre

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/alaska-sale/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i47FW9FEceQ
Published: 2026-11-22 · Duration: 0:37 · Place: Alaska
Short answer: Why did Russia sell Alaska? In 1867 it was hard to defend, far from St Petersburg and next door to British Canada, so Russia sold it to the United States for $7.2 million: about two cents an acre. Today Alaska pumps $7 million worth of oil every few hours.

Key facts:
- Purchase price: $7,200,000 (The sum the United States agreed to pay Russia for Alaska in 1867.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Treaty signed: March 30, 1867 (Signed in Washington by US Secretary of State William Seward and Russian minister Eduard de Stoeckl, at 4 a.m. after negotiating through the night.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Senate vote: 37 to 2 (The US Senate ratified the treaty on April 9, 1867.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Formal handover: October 18, 1867 (In Sitka, the Russian flag was lowered and the US flag was raised.) [source: US Office of the Historian]
- Price per acre: About 2 cents (Roughly 1,518,800 km² (375 million acres) for $7.2 million works out to about 1.9 cents an acre.)
- Size compared with France: About 2.7 times (Alaska has about 1,481,346 km² of land, against about 543,940 km² for metropolitan France.)
- Prudhoe Bay oil discovery: Announced March 12, 1968 (Prudhoe Bay is the largest oil field in the United States.) [source: National Park Service]
- Alaska oil output in 2026: About 413,000–428,000 barrels a day (At around $100 a barrel, that is roughly $7 million worth of oil every four hours.) [source: US Energy Information Administration]

### Why Russia Sold Alaska to the United States in 1867

Russia sold Alaska because it was hard to defend and Russia feared losing it to Britain in a future war. In 1867 it agreed to sell the territory to the United States for **$7.2 million**, about two cents an acre. Today Alaska produces that much money in oil every few hours.

## What was Alaska before 1867?

Before the sale, the land was a Russian colony known as *Russian America*. The name "Alaska" was chosen by the United States after the purchase.

It was enormous. Alaska has about 1,481,346 km² of land, roughly **2.7 times** the size of metropolitan France. The area covered by the treaty was about 1,518,800 km², or some 375 million acres.

## Why did Russia want to sell Alaska?

After its defeat in the Crimean War, Russia saw Alaska as difficult to defend. Historians point to one main concern: in a future war, British forces could take the territory easily from neighbouring Canada. In 1867 the land to the east, including the Yukon, was British territory.

According to the US Office of the Historian, selling to the United States was a way to offset the designs of Great Britain in the region. If Russia was going to lose Alaska, it preferred that the United States have it.

## How did the deal happen?

The treaty was negotiated by US Secretary of State **William Seward** and the Russian minister in Washington, **Eduard de Stoeckl**. After talks that ran through the night, they signed it in Washington at 4 a.m. on **March 30, 1867**.

The US Senate ratified it on **April 9, 1867**, by a vote of 37 to 2. The formal handover took place in **Sitka on October 18, 1867**, when the Russian flag came down and the US flag went up.

## How much did the United States pay?

The price was **$7,200,000**. Divided over roughly 375 million acres, that comes to about 1.9 cents an acre, or around two cents. Adjusted with the consumer price index, $7.2 million in 1867 is roughly **$164 million** in 2026 dollars.

## Was the Alaska Purchase called Seward's Folly?

Yes, by some. Critics dubbed it *Seward's Folly* and *Seward's Icebox*, mocking the idea of paying for a frozen land. Those nicknames stuck, but they did not reflect the whole picture: most of the press at the time supported the purchase.

## What happened after the sale?

First came gold. The first major strike in Alaska was at Anvil Creek, near Nome, on September 20, 1898, and the Nome gold rush ran from 1899 to 1909.

Then came oil. The discovery at **Prudhoe Bay** was announced on March 12, 1968. It is the largest oil field in the United States.

## How much oil does Alaska produce today?

In 2026 Alaska has been producing around 413,000 to 428,000 barrels a day, and Alaska North Slope crude has traded at around $100 or more. At about 420,000 barrels and $100 a barrel, that is roughly $42 million a day, or about $7.2 million every four hours. Even at much lower prices, such as $55 a barrel, it would take only around seven and a half hours.

So who got the better deal? Russia sold a territory it believed it could not hold. The United States bought land whose value only became clear decades later.

## Key takeaways

- Russia sold Alaska in 1867 because it was hard to defend and Russia feared losing it to Britain.
- The price was $7.2 million, about two cents an acre.
- The treaty was signed on March 30, 1867, and Alaska was handed over in Sitka on October 18, 1867.
- Critics called it *Seward's Folly*, though most of the press supported it.
- Gold near Nome and oil at Prudhoe Bay later made Alaska far more valuable than its purchase price.

FAQ:
Q: Why did Russia sell Alaska?
A: Russia sold Alaska because it was hard to defend and Russia feared British forces in Canada would take it in a future war. It preferred to sell it to the United States instead.
Q: How much did the US pay for Alaska?
A: The United States paid $7.2 million in 1867, about two cents an acre. That is roughly $164 million in 2026 dollars when adjusted for inflation.
Q: When did Alaska become part of the United States?
A: The purchase treaty was signed on March 30, 1867, and ratified by the Senate on April 9, 1867. The formal transfer took place in Sitka on October 18, 1867.

Transcript:

Rewind to 1867. This is Russian America.
Almost three times the size of France.
But it's hard to defend, and Russia fears Britain will grab it.
So it offers a deal to the United States.
Russia: Seven point two million. Deal?
United States: Deal!
That's two cents an acre.

Then come gold… and oil.
Today, Alaska pumps seven million dollars of oil every few hours.
And to think…

Sources: US Office of the Historian; National Park Service; US Energy Information Administration; Alaska Department of Revenue

## How Much of Ukraine Does Russia Control?

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/ukraine-front/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FRN2bWGVwTU
Published: 2026-11-21 · Duration: 0:37 · Place: Ukraine
Short answer: How much of Ukraine does Russia control? About 19% in November 2026, according to DeepStateMap: roughly 114,000 km², an area bigger than Portugal. We rewind the map to 2013 and watch the front line move, month by month.

Key facts:
- Share of Ukraine controlled by Russia (17 Nov 2026): About 19% (19.2% of Ukraine including Crimea, based on the DeepStateMap snapshot of 17 November 2026.) [source: DeepStateMap (deepstatemap.live), monthly snapshots to 17 Nov 2026]
- Area controlled by Russia (17 Nov 2026): About 114,000 km² (114,449 km² in the 17 November 2026 snapshot, more than the whole of Portugal (92,225 km²).) [source: DeepStateMap (deepstatemap.live), monthly snapshots to 17 Nov 2026]
- Annexation of Crimea: 18 March 2014 (The date the treaty annexing Crimea to Russia was signed.) [source: Britannica]
- Fighting in the Donbas: April 2014 (Russian troops and Russian-backed local forces took part of the Donbas; the line there was stable from February 2015.) [source: Britannica]
- Full-scale invasion: 24 February 2022 (Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.) [source: Britannica]
- Peak of Russian control (March 2022): Over a fifth (Estimates range from about 21% (around 133,000 km²) to 27% depending on the source.) [source: ISW]
- Share controlled by Russia (December 2022): 17.7% (After Ukraine retook ground around Kyiv, Kharkiv and Kherson in 2022, the figure rose slowly to 19.2% by November 2026.) [source: DeepStateMap (deepstatemap.live), monthly snapshots to 17 Nov 2026]

### Ukraine's Front Line from 2014 to 2026, Month by Month

As of 17 November 2026, Russia controls about 19% of Ukraine, according to DeepStateMap: roughly 114,000 km², including Crimea. That is an area larger than the whole of Portugal. The figure is the result of more than a decade of change, from the annexation of Crimea in 2014 to the full-scale invasion of 2022 and the slow movement of the front line since.

*All front-line figures on this page refer to the date given. The line keeps moving, so later figures may differ.*

## How much of Ukraine does Russia control today?

In the DeepStateMap snapshot of 17 November 2026, Russia controlled 114,449 km², or 19.2% of Ukraine including Crimea. Measured against Ukraine's official area of 603,550 km², the share is 19.0%.

Other trackers give similar figures. Russia Matters, using DeepStateMap data to 11 November 2026, put it at about 45,227 square miles, roughly 117,100 km², or "about 19% of Ukraine". The Council on Foreign Relations' Global Conflict Tracker describes it as roughly 20 percent.

For scale: Portugal covers 92,225 km² including its islands. The area under Russian control in November 2026 is larger than all of it.

## What happened in 2014?

In 2013, the whole of Ukraine, including Crimea, was under Ukrainian control. That changed in 2014.

- **March 2014:** Russia annexed Crimea. The annexation treaty was signed on 18 March 2014.
- **April 2014:** Russian troops and Russian-backed local forces took control of part of the Donbas, in eastern Ukraine.
- **February 2015:** after the fighting around Debaltseve, the line in the Donbas became largely stable.

## What changed in 2022?

On 24 February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with forces advancing from the north, the east and the south.

Russian control peaked in March 2022. Estimates of that peak vary by source, from about 21% of the country (around 133,000 km², according to ISW) to 27% (according to Al Jazeera). Either way, Russia held over a fifth of Ukraine at that point.

## Where did Ukraine retake territory?

Ukraine pushed back in three main areas during 2022:

- **Around Kyiv:** Russian forces withdrew from the north in April 2022.
- **Around Kharkiv:** a Ukrainian counteroffensive in September 2022 retook ground in the region.
- **Around Kherson:** Ukraine retook Kherson on 11 November 2022.

By December 2022, the share of Ukraine under Russian control had fallen to 17.7%.

## How has the front line moved since 2023?

Since then, the changes have been gradual. Month by month, Russian forces have advanced slowly, village by village, notably on the Donetsk front. The share of Ukraine under Russian control rose from 17.7% in December 2022 to 19.2% in November 2026.

The front line is still moving, which is why every figure on this page is tied to a date.

## Key takeaways

- As of 17 November 2026, Russia controls about 19% of Ukraine (114,449 km², including Crimea), according to DeepStateMap.
- That area is larger than Portugal (92,225 km²).
- Russia annexed Crimea in March 2014; Russian-backed forces took part of the Donbas the same year.
- The full-scale invasion began on 24 February 2022; at its peak in March 2022, Russia held over a fifth of the country.
- Ukraine retook ground around Kyiv, Kharkiv and Kherson in 2022, bringing the figure to 17.7% by December 2022.
- Since then, the share has risen slowly to 19.2% by November 2026.

FAQ:
Q: How much of Ukraine does Russia control in 2026?
A: About 19% as of 17 November 2026, according to DeepStateMap: 114,449 km² including Crimea. That is an area larger than Portugal.
Q: When did Russia annex Crimea?
A: In March 2014. The annexation treaty was signed on 18 March 2014, and in April 2014 Russian-backed forces also took part of the Donbas.
Q: What was the most territory Russia held in Ukraine?
A: Over a fifth of the country, at the peak in March 2022, shortly after the full-scale invasion of 24 February 2022. Estimates range from about 21% to 27% depending on the source.

Sources: DeepStateMap (deepstatemap.live), monthly snapshots to 17 Nov 2026

## The True Size of Africa: US, India and EU Fit

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/africa-size/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6WHdqIvEl5o
Published: 2026-11-20 · Duration: 0:36 · Place: Africa
Short answer: What is the true size of Africa? On a Mercator map Greenland looks just as big, but Africa is 14 times larger: the mainland US, India and all 27 EU countries fit inside it at the same time, with almost half the continent to spare.

Key facts:
- Area of Africa: About 30.4 million km² (Estimates range from 30,365,000 to 30,370,000 km² depending on the source.) [source: Britannica]
- Area of Greenland: 2,166,086 km² (On a Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Africa compared with Greenland: 14 times bigger (Africa's area divided by Greenland's comes out at about 14.) [source: Britannica]
- Mercator projection: 1569 (Drawn by Gerardus Mercator for navigators; it enlarges areas about 4 times at 60° latitude and about 10.5 times at 72°.)
- Mainland United States: 8,080,464 km² (The 48 contiguous states plus DC, without Alaska or Hawaii.) [source: US Census Bureau]
- India: 3,287,263 km² (The second country placed inside Africa in the comparison.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- European Union (27 countries): 4,236,351 km² (All 27 member states fit inside Africa together with the US and India.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Share of Africa still uncovered: Almost half (The three together cover 15,604,078 km², about 51% of Africa, leaving about 49% free.) [source: fit measured on Natural Earth outlines]

### Mercator vs Reality: How Big Africa Actually Is

Africa covers about 30.4 million km², roughly 14 times the area of Greenland, even though the two look about the same size on the world map most people know. Africa is so large that the mainland United States, India and all 27 countries of the European Union fit inside it at the same time, and almost half of the continent is still left uncovered.

## Why does Africa look smaller than it is?

The map most of us grew up with uses the Mercator projection, drawn by Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for navigators. To flatten a round globe into a rectangle, it stretches everything that lies far from the equator.

The stretching grows fast as you move towards the poles. At 60 degrees of latitude, areas look about 4 times bigger than they really are. At 72 degrees, they look about 10.5 times bigger.

Mercator has never gone away. Online maps such as Google Maps use a version of it called Web Mercator, so it is still the picture of the world many people see every day.

Africa lies across the equator, where Mercator distorts least. Greenland, Canada and Russia lie far to the north, where it distorts most.

## Is Greenland really as big as Africa?

No. On a Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa, but that is the projection at work.

Greenland covers 2,166,086 km². Africa covers about 30.4 million km². Divide one by the other and you get roughly 14. Slide Greenland down to the equator, where the map stops stretching it, and it shrinks into a small patch inside Africa.

## What countries fit inside Africa?

To show how big Africa really is, we placed three large pieces of the world inside it, all at once and without overlapping:

- **The mainland United States:** 8,080,464 km², meaning the 48 contiguous states plus DC, without Alaska or Hawaii.
- **India:** 3,287,263 km².
- **The European Union:** 4,236,351 km² across all 27 member states.

Together they add up to 15,604,078 km², about 51% of Africa. That leaves roughly 49% of the continent, almost half, still uncovered.

## How was the fit checked?

The comparison is not an artist's sketch. The fit was measured on Natural Earth outlines, moving each country across the globe without stretching or distorting its shape, only allowing it to rotate.

A few choices keep it fair:

- Africa means the mainland only, without Madagascar, small islands or the Sinai Peninsula.
- The United States means the 48 contiguous states.
- India is shown without the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
- EU countries are shown with their European territory only, without the Canary Islands, the Azores, Madeira or overseas regions.

With those outlines, all 29 pieces fit inside mainland Africa with 0 km² sticking out past the coast and 0 km² of overlap between them.

## Key takeaways

- Africa covers about 30.4 million km², around 14 times the size of Greenland.
- The Mercator projection (1569) stretches land far from the equator, which is why Greenland looks as big as Africa.
- The mainland US, India and all 27 EU countries fit inside Africa at the same time.
- Those three together cover about 51% of Africa, leaving almost half uncovered.
- The fit was measured on real outlines, with no overlap and nothing outside the coast.

FAQ:
Q: How much bigger is Africa than Greenland?
A: About 14 times bigger. Africa covers about 30.4 million km² and Greenland 2,166,086 km², even though they look similar on a Mercator map.
Q: Why does Greenland look so big on maps?
A: Because most world maps use the Mercator projection, which stretches everything far from the equator. At 60° latitude areas look about 4 times larger than they really are, and at 72° about 10.5 times larger.
Q: Can the US, India and Europe fit inside Africa?
A: Yes. The mainland US, India and all 27 EU countries fit inside Africa at the same time, without overlapping, and almost half of the continent is still left uncovered.

Transcript:

So Greenland looks as big as Africa.
Now slide it down to the equator.
Africa is fourteen times bigger.
So what fits inside? The mainland US…
United States: Wait. I'm the small one?
India…

So next time you see this map…

Sources: Britannica; CIA World Factbook; US Census Bureau; fit measured on Natural Earth outlines

## Lesotho: The Country Inside South Africa

URL: https://globetape.github.io/videos/lesotho/
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJLDw3Rc5ns
Published: 2026-11-19 · Duration: 0:36 · Place: Lesotho
Short answer: Why is Lesotho inside South Africa? It's a whole independent country, about the size of Belgium, completely surrounded by a single neighbour. Even its lowest point sits 1,400 metres above sea level: a world record.

Key facts:
- Area of Lesotho: 30,355 km² (A fully independent country, completely surrounded by South Africa.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Area of Belgium, for comparison: 30,689 km² (Lesotho and Belgium are almost exactly the same size.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Lowest point in Lesotho: About 1,400 m (The highest lowest point of any country in the world.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- British protection: 1868 (King Moshoeshoe I asked Britain for protection, and the territory became the protectorate of Basutoland.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Union of South Africa: 1910 (Basutoland stayed outside the Union of South Africa and never joined it.)
- Independence: 4 October 1966 (Basutoland became the independent country of Lesotho.) [source: CIA World Factbook]
- Countries entirely surrounded by one other country: 3 (Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City.)

### How Lesotho Ended Up Surrounded by South Africa

Lesotho is inside South Africa because of a decision taken more than 150 years ago. It is a fully independent country of 30,355 km², about the size of Belgium, and South Africa surrounds it completely. In 1868 its king asked Britain for protection; in 1910 the territory, then called Basutoland, stayed outside the Union of South Africa; and on 4 October 1966 it became independent as Lesotho.

## Where exactly is Lesotho?

Look at a map of southern Africa and you will spot a hole in the middle of South Africa. That hole is not a lake or a nature reserve. It is a separate country with its own government and its own borders: Lesotho.

What makes it unusual is that it has only one neighbour. Every kilometre of its border is shared with South Africa. Geographers call this an enclave: a country entirely surrounded by a single other country.

## How big is Lesotho?

Lesotho covers 30,355 km². Belgium covers 30,689 km². The two are almost exactly the same size.

So Lesotho is not a tiny city-state tucked into a corner of the map. It is a country the size of a European nation, sitting completely inside its larger neighbour.

## Why is Lesotho's lowest point a world record?

Lesotho holds a genuine world record. Its lowest point is about 1,400 metres above sea level, the highest lowest point of any country on Earth.

In practical terms, there is nowhere in Lesotho that sits lower than roughly 1,400 metres. Even the bottom of the country is high ground: the whole of Lesotho sits well above sea level.

## Why did Lesotho never become part of South Africa?

The answer is in its history. Three dates explain most of it:

- **1868:** King Moshoeshoe I asked Britain for protection. The territory became the British protectorate of Basutoland.
- **1910:** The Union of South Africa came together, and Basutoland stayed outside it.
- **4 October 1966:** Basutoland became independent and took the name Lesotho.

British protection put Basutoland on a separate track from its neighbours. When the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, Basutoland was not part of it, and it never joined afterwards. By the time it became independent in 1966, the borders were already set. The result is the map we see today: an independent country with a single neighbour on every side.

## Are there other countries completely surrounded by another country?

Yes, but very few. Only three countries on Earth are entirely surrounded by one other country. Lesotho is one of them. The other two are San Marino and Vatican City.

That makes Lesotho a true geographic rarity: one of just three countries in the world that cannot reach any other nation without first crossing a single neighbour.

## Key takeaways

- Lesotho is an independent country completely surrounded by South Africa.
- It covers 30,355 km², about the same as Belgium (30,689 km²).
- Its lowest point is about 1,400 metres above sea level, a world record.
- In 1868 King Moshoeshoe I asked Britain for protection, creating Basutoland.
- Basutoland stayed outside the Union of South Africa in 1910 and became independent as Lesotho on 4 October 1966.
- Only three countries are surrounded by a single country: Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City.

FAQ:
Q: Why is Lesotho inside South Africa?
A: Because of its history: in 1868 its king, Moshoeshoe I, asked Britain for protection, and the territory became Basutoland. It stayed outside the Union of South Africa in 1910 and became independent as Lesotho in 1966, still surrounded on every side by South Africa.
Q: How big is Lesotho compared to Belgium?
A: They are almost the same size. Lesotho covers 30,355 km² and Belgium covers 30,689 km².
Q: Which countries are completely surrounded by another country?
A: Only three: Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City. Lesotho is the one surrounded by South Africa.

Lesotho: Hi!

…and South Africa surrounds it completely.
South Africa: You're welcome.

Sources: CIA World Factbook
